rules.description: Repeated authentication failures indicate credential brute forcing. Confidence medium: a single failure event alone cannot distinguish an attack from a typo; the sequence correlator raises certainty.

evidence: Authentication failure event detected.
Repeated failed login activity may indicate brute force behavior.
investigation: Check source IP frequency.
Review failed login count per account.
Verify whether MFA or account lockout controls were triggered.

rules.description: An accepted SSH login is use of a valid account; legitimacy requires review. Matches on log text so transports classified under other event types still map.

evidence: SSH accepted-login pattern detected.
Valid account usage may require legitimacy review.
investigation: Confirm whether the login was expected.
Review source IP reputation and geolocation.
Check for follow-on activity after login.

evidence: An interactive SSH session was established.
If the source is an internal host, SSH is the classic lateral-movement transport.
investigation: Determine whether the source host is internal or external.
For an internal source, review that host for prior compromise indicators.

rules.description: The classifier's arp-spoofing event type: adversary-in-the-middle positioning on the local segment. Parent technique first (the event alone proves AiTM intent), ARP cache poisoning as the refined sub-technique.

evidence: ARP cache-poisoning indicator detected (IP-to-MAC binding changed unexpectedly).
ARP poisoning positions an attacker to intercept or relay traffic on the local segment.
investigation: Identify the MAC address claiming the disputed IP and locate the physical port it is attached to.
Check whether DHCP lease churn or a virtual-IP failover explains the rebinding before treating it as hostile.
Review traffic captured during the window for credential or session data exposed in cleartext.

evidence: The observed mechanism (gratuitous ARP rebinding) is specifically ARP cache poisoning.
investigation: Enable dynamic ARP inspection or equivalent on the affected segment if available.

rules.description: Log-text fallback for ARP cache-poisoning indicators when the event type is generic (e.g. an IDS alert about ARP activity). Same attribution as arp-spoofing-event; the engine merges duplicates.

evidence: ARP cache-poisoning indicator detected (IP-to-MAC binding changed unexpectedly).
ARP poisoning positions an attacker to intercept or relay traffic on the local segment.
investigation: Identify the MAC address claiming the disputed IP and locate the physical port it is attached to.
Check whether DHCP lease churn or a virtual-IP failover explains the rebinding before treating it as hostile.
Review traffic captured during the window for credential or session data exposed in cleartext.

evidence: The observed mechanism (gratuitous ARP rebinding) is specifically ARP cache poisoning.
investigation: Enable dynamic ARP inspection or equivalent on the affected segment if available.

rules.description: Audit-evidence destruction. ATT&CK v19 places indicator removal under the Stealth tactic (Defense Evasion was split into Stealth and Defense Impairment in v19).

evidence: Audit-evidence destruction indicator detected (history cleared, log removed, or audit daemon stopped).
Clearing evidence is post-compromise behavior — it presumes there was activity worth hiding.
investigation: Recover the audit trail from remote or forwarded log copies.
Establish what the account did before the evidence was cleared.
Treat the host as compromised until the review completes.

rules.description: Membership in sudo/wheel/admin grants durable elevated access — an escalation and persistence primitive.

evidence: An account was added to a privileged group (sudo/wheel/admin).
Privileged-group membership grants durable elevated access — a persistence and escalation primitive.
investigation: Verify the change against change-management records.
Check when the target account was created — a fresh account gaining privilege is the classic persistence chain.
Review the actor account that performed the change.

rules.description: Local account creation as a persistence mechanism. The classifier's markers (useradd, new user/account) prove a local account specifically, so the sub-technique is warranted.

evidence: A local account was created.
Adversaries create local accounts to maintain access that survives credential rotation.
investigation: Confirm the account maps to an approved provisioning request.
Watch for follow-on privilege changes on the same account.
Review the creating account's session for other changes.

rules.description: Service discovery commonly precedes exploitation of the services it enumerates.

evidence: Port-scanning activity detected (service discovery probes).
Service discovery commonly precedes exploitation of the services it enumerates.
investigation: Identify the scan source and whether it is an authorized scanner (vulnerability management, asset inventory).
Review exposure of the probed ports and their services.
Correlate with follow-on connection attempts from the same source.

rules.description: Any successful login the classifier surfaces as a security event maps to Valid Accounts pending legitimacy review — coverage the transport-specific SSH rule alone missed.

evidence: A successful login was surfaced as a security event.
Valid account usage may require legitimacy review.
investigation: Confirm whether the login was expected.
Review source IP reputation and geolocation.
Check for follow-on activity after login.

rules.description: A generic IDS alert cannot be attributed to a technique without signature and packet context — an explicit review sentinel, never a guess.

evidence: IDS alert requires signature and packet-context review.
investigation: Review IDS signature metadata.
Correlate with destination asset exposure.
Inspect packet capture if available.

evidence: No supported mapping rule matched.
investigation: Review raw log evidence.
Add a new mapping rule if pattern becomes repeatable.
